boundary_rationale: The unit opens on the command “Go, and buy yourself a linen belt” (web:Jer.13.1), a Yahweh-to-Jeremiah instruction fronted by כֹּֽה אָמַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה אֵלַ֗י הָל֞וֹךְ (oshb:Jer.13.1, byte tier) -- the koh-amar shape used here as narrative preterite rather than a public oracle formula. A second word-event opens the burial command at 13:3 (‘the second time’), and the interpretation phase opens with its own word-event at 13:8, וַיְהִ֥י דְבַר יְהוָ֖ה אֵלַ֥י לֵאמֹֽר (oshb:Jer.13.8, byte tier). Command (13:1-2), the burial-and-recovery performance (13:3-7), and the interpretation (13:8-11, closing “the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah to cling to me”, web:Jer.13.11) stay one unit because no addressee or scene shift interrupts the sequence -- the scene keeps the same two participants, Jeremiah and the belt, from command to interpretation, and both internal word-event onsets mark phases of the same enacted sign rather than a fresh oracle to a new audience.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 13:3 and 13:8 as separate rows (one per word-event onset) was weighed and set aside: both introduce a phase of the same enacted sign rather than a change of addressee or scene, and a symbolic act's command, performance, and interpretation stay one unit unless a tier-1 seam of that kind intervenes.
literature_type_guess: enacted sign-act narrative: a worn-then-buried loincloth as a ruined emblem of covenant pride
wj_or_red_letter_considered: not applicable in the OT substrate
device_notes: Jer.12.17 carries a setumah just before the opening (single-witness, tier-3 in the Prophets). Within the span, Jer.13.2 carries a further setumah and Jer.13.7 a petuchah -- texture, not a driver of this boundary.

boundary_rationale: A fresh discourse-frame imperative opens the row: “Therefore you shall speak to them this word” (web:Jer.13.12), spliced וְאָמַרְתָּ֨ אֲלֵיהֶ֜ם אֶת הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֗ה (oshb:Jer.13.12, byte tier) -- Yahweh commissioning Jeremiah to relay a new saying, distinct from the belt's own interpretation just given. The commissioned proverb, “Every container should be filled with wine” (web:Jer.13.12), turns into a judgment against “the kings who sit on David’s throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (web:Jer.13.13), closing at 13:14 with the neum-YHWH formula marking the unit's end.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this proverb-oracle into the preceding sign-act row was considered: both concern the same belt-owning voice, but 13:12 opens its own commissioned-speech imperative rather than continuing the belt's interpretation, so the two stay separate.
literature_type_guess: riddle-proverb turned judgment oracle: wine-jars saying applied to national drunkenness
wj_or_red_letter_considered: not applicable in the OT substrate
device_notes: Jer.13.12 carries a setumah, and Jer.13.14 -- the row's own close -- carries a further setumah (WLC, single-witness, tier-3 weak in the Prophets).

boundary_rationale: “Hear, and give ear” (web:Jer.13.15), rendering שִׁמְע֥וּ וְהַאֲזִ֖ינוּ (oshb:Jer.13.15, byte tier), opens a fresh imperative address to the audience distinct from the commissioned proverb just closed. The call to give Yahweh glory before darkness falls (13:16) shifts in 13:17 into first-person prophetic grief -- “my soul will weep in secret for your pride” -- without any addressee or scene change, so the weeping stays inside this warning rather than opening a fresh unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Labeling this row lament_confession on the strength of 13:17's first-person weeping was considered and set aside: the enumerated confession and communal-lament spans do not include 13:17, and the weeping here sits inside a warning addressed outward to the audience rather than a petition addressed to Yahweh.
literature_type_guess: warning oracle with embedded prophetic weeping over threatened exile
wj_or_red_letter_considered: not applicable in the OT substrate
device_notes: Jer.13.14, just before this row, carries a setumah; Jer.13.17, the row's own close, carries a second setumah (WLC, single-witness, tier-3 in the Prophets).

boundary_rationale: “Say to the king and to the queen mother” (web:Jer.13.18) opens on אֱמֹ֥ר לַמֶּ֛לֶךְ וְלַגְּבִירָ֖ה (oshb:Jer.13.18, byte tier), a discourse imperative naming a new addressee pair -- the king and the queen mother -- distinct from the plural audience of 13:15-17. The two verses form one short oracle: the royal pair's fallen crown (13:18) and Judah's captivity (13:19) belong to the same announcement, with no further seam between them.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running 13:18-19 together with the material that follows through 13:27 as one royal-and-national poem was considered: the addressee shifts again at 13:20 to a second-feminine-singular Jerusalem figure, a distinct enough referent from the king and the queen mother to keep the two apart, though the case for reading it as one sustained poem is not without force.
literature_type_guess: royal humiliation oracle addressed to the king and the queen mother

boundary_rationale: The address turns to a second-feminine-singular figure at 13:20 -- “Lift up your eyes, and see those who come from the north” (web:Jer.13.20) renders הַבָּאִ֖ים מִצָּפ֑וֹן (oshb:Jer.13.20, byte tier) -- distinct from the king-and-queen-mother pair just addressed. (13:20 also carries a doubled ketiv/qere note on its two opening imperatives, consulted but not spliced here.) The sustained indictment of Jerusalem-as-woman runs through the scattering sentence (13:24-25) and the uncovering of her skirts (13:26) to the closing apostrophe: “Woe to you, Jerusalem” (web:Jer.13.27), where א֥וֹי לָךְ֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם (oshb:Jer.13.27, byte tier) is the oy lexeme (sweep: 8 verses book-wide) -- a different word from the vav-prefixed hoy that opens the woe oracles at 22:13 and 23:1, so this row is not typed woe_oracle.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Joining 13:20-27 to the preceding royal oracle (13:18-19) into one ten-verse row was considered: the shift from a plural/2ms royal address to a sustained 2fs Jerusalem address is real, but the two share the same humiliation-and-exposure imagery, so the fold-together reading is not unreasonable.
literature_type_guess: Jerusalem-as-adulteress indictment closing in a funeral-toned apostrophe

device_notes: Jer.13.19 carries a setumah just ahead of this row's opening; Jer.13.27, where the row ends, carries a petuchah (WLC, single-witness, tier-3 weak in the Prophets).

boundary_rationale: “This is Yahweh’s word that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought” (web:Jer.14.1) renders the asher-hayah debar-YHWH el-Yirmeyahu header אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָיָ֤ה דְבַר יְהוָה֙ אֶֽל יִרְמְיָ֔הוּ עַל דִּבְרֵ֖י (oshb:Jer.14.1, byte tier) -- the OAN/topical-header shape, attested at four sites book-wide (sweep: 4 verses: 14:1, 46:1, 47:1, 49:34). The header is kept with the drought description that follows (14:2-6: mourning gates, dry cisterns, cracked ground, the doe forsaking her fawn, the wild donkeys panting) rather than standing alone, matching how the header-bounded units elsewhere in the book carry their attached content as one piece. Framed here as judgment_oracle by its dominant content -- a report of covenant devastation already unfolding -- rather than superscription, since only one of the six verses is the bare title.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating 14:1 as its own one-verse superscription row, separate from the drought description, was considered and set aside in favor of the larger bundled unit, since the description carries the row's substance and no addressee shift separates the header from what it introduces.
literature_type_guess: topical word-event header opening a drought-devastation report
wj_or_red_letter_considered: not applicable in the OT substrate
device_notes: Jer.13.27, just before this row, carries a petuchah (single-witness, tier-3 WLC corroboration in the Prophets). No verse within 14:1-6 itself carries a parashah mark.

boundary_rationale: The voice turns first-person plural and direct-address at 14:7: “Though our iniquities testify against us, work for your name’s sake, Yahweh” (web:Jer.14.7) spliced אִם עֲוֺנֵ֨ינוּ֙ עָ֣נוּ (oshb:Jer.14.7, byte tier) -- a scene shift from the third-person drought description just given to the people's own plea. The petition (our rebellions, our sins) and the appeal to Yahweh as “the hope of Israel” (14:8) run through the closing plea “don’t leave us” (14:9), a bounded communal cry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row backward to include the drought description (14:1-6) was considered: both concern the same distress, but the shift from third-person report to first-person-plural direct address to Yahweh is a scene change strong enough to keep the plea as its own unit.
literature_type_guess: communal penitential plea invoking Yahweh's name
wj_or_red_letter_considered: not applicable in the OT substrate
device_notes: Jer.14.9, this row's own close, carries a setumah (WLC, single-witness, tier-3 weak in the Prophets). Jer.14.6, just before the opening, is unmarked.

boundary_rationale: “Yahweh says to this people” (web:Jer.14.10) carries כֹּֽה אָמַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה לָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֗ה (oshb:Jer.14.10, byte tier), Yahweh answering the plea just voiced with a pronouncement spoken about the people in the third person rather than to them or to Jeremiah alone -- a distinct footing from both the communal plea before it and the private address to Jeremiah that opens next at 14:11. This one verse closes its own thought: remembered iniquity, punished sin.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this verse into the communal plea that precedes it, as the divine answer completing one exchange, was considered: the topic (the people's fate) carries over from 14:7-9, but the addressee shifts from Yahweh-as-hearer to the people-as-subject, which this row keeps separate.
literature_type_guess: one-verse divine refusal oracle answering the people's plea

device_notes: Jer.14.9, just before this row, carries a setumah; Jer.14.10, the row's own verse, carries a further setumah (single-witness, tier-3 WLC corroboration in the Prophets).

boundary_rationale: “Yahweh said to me” (web:Jer.14.11) opens וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוָ֖ה אֵלָ֑י אַל תִּתְפַּלֵּ֛ל (oshb:Jer.14.11, byte tier) -- a scene shift to private address to Jeremiah, instructing him not to intercede, distinct from 14:10's pronouncement about the people at large. “Then I said” (web:Jer.14.13) is Jeremiah's own protest within that same exchange, citing prophets who promise “assured peace”; Yahweh's reply exposing the lying prophets runs through 14:14-16 without a further addressee change, so the whole exchange stays one row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the row at 14:13 (Jeremiah's protest) or at 14:14 (Yahweh's extended reply) was considered: both are speaker turns within one sustained private exchange, and neither carries an addressee or scene change of its own, so the dialogue was kept whole.
literature_type_guess: private dialogue oracle exposing the lying prophets

boundary_rationale: A fresh discourse-frame imperative opens the row: “You shall say this word to them” (web:Jer.14.17), rendering וְאָמַרְתָּ֤ אֲלֵיהֶם֙ אֶת הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה (oshb:Jer.14.17, byte tier) -- words given to Jeremiah to speak, distinct from the exchange about the lying prophets just closed. The commissioned dirge over “the virgin daughter of my people” runs through 14:18's slain-by-sword and sick-with-famine pairing, ending on “prophet and priest... have no knowledge.”
strongest_rejected_alternative: Labeling this row lament_confession for its weeping register was considered and set aside: it is not among the enumerated confession or communal-lament spans, and its content -- sword and famine as accomplished fact -- announces judgment even though voiced as mourning.
literature_type_guess: commissioned dirge over the sword-and-famine dead

boundary_rationale: “Have you utterly rejected Judah” (web:Jer.14.19) opens הֲמָאֹ֨ס מָאַ֜סְתָּ אֶת יְהוּדָ֗ה (oshb:Jer.14.19, byte tier) -- the voice returns to first-person-plural direct address to Yahweh, a scene shift from the commissioned dirge just closed back to the people's own petition. “We acknowledge, Yahweh, our wickedness” (14:20) and the appeal to the rain-giving Creator (14:22) carry the plea to its close, a bounded communal cry paired with the one at 14:7-9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row forward into 15:1 (Yahweh's reply) was considered: 15:1 does answer the plea just voiced, but it is addressed to Jeremiah rather than to Yahweh, a scene change kept as the start of a separate row.

boundary_rationale: “Then Yahweh said to me” (web:Jer.15.1) opens וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֵלַ֔י אִם יַעֲמֹ֨ד מֹשֶׁ֤ה וּשְׁמוּאֵל֙ (oshb:Jer.15.1, byte tier) -- private address to Jeremiah answering the plea just closed, naming Moses and Samuel as intercessors who could not turn back the sentence. The four-fold assignment to death, sword, famine, and captivity (15:2-3) and the Manasseh clause (15:4) continue the same divine speech to Jeremiah without a further addressee change.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 15:1-4 as the closing movement of the communal plea at 14:19-22 rather than a separate row was considered: 15:1 replies to that plea in substance, but it addresses Jeremiah, not Yahweh, which this tiling treats as the more decisive discourse signal.
literature_type_guess: Moses-and-Samuel oracle of irrevocable four-fold judgment

boundary_rationale: “For who will have pity on you, Jerusalem?” (web:Jer.15.5) turns to second-feminine-singular direct address, כִּ֠י מִֽי יַחְמֹ֤ל עָלַ֨יִךְ֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם (oshb:Jer.15.5, byte tier) -- Jerusalem addressed by name rather than by the third-person language of 15:1-4. The poem moves between that direct address (15:5-6) and third-person description of the widows and the destroyer (15:7-9) without a further scene change, closing on the neum-YHWH formula at 15:9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the row where the grammar shifts from second-person address (15:5-6) to third-person description (15:7-9) was considered: Hebrew poetry moves between address and description within one sustained poem routinely, so no fresh row was opened there.
literature_type_guess: direct-address dirge over Jerusalem's bereaved widows

boundary_rationale: “Woe is me, my mother” (web:Jer.15.10) opens אֽוֹי לִ֣י אִמִּ֔י כִּ֣י יְלִדְתִּ֗נִי (oshb:Jer.15.10, byte tier) -- another oy apostrophe (sweep: 8 verses book-wide, the same lexeme spliced at 13:27 above), here turned inward as Jeremiah's own outcry rather than a judgment against the city, a clean scene shift from the divine judgment speech just closed. Yahweh's reply opens at 15:11 without a further addressee change (private dialogue continues), and a second reply opens “Therefore Yahweh says” (web:Jer.15.19) on לָכֵ֞ן כֹּֽה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה (oshb:Jer.15.19, byte tier) -- a koh-amar with no change of frame-owner, so it does not itself open a fresh row. Complaint and reply run together to the closing promise of deliverance at 15:21.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting the row at 15:19's koh-amar onset, or at 15:11 where the voice turns from Jeremiah's complaint to Yahweh's reply, was considered and set aside: the confession's complaint-and-reply dialogue holds one scene and one addressee pair, Jeremiah and Yahweh, from complaint to reply, and 15:19's koh-amar does not change the frame-owner from the reply already underway.
literature_type_guess: individual complaint-and-reply dialogue between Jeremiah and Yahweh
